info.text:
The Great Recession began in December 2007, but it wasn't made official until December 1, 2008. This video explains how the NBER defines and dates recessions (and why two shrinking GDP quarters, like those reported in 2022, is only a rule of thumb), every US recession since 1973 with its length, and the four triggers history keeps repeating: oil shocks, Fed tightening, bursting bubbles and sudden shocks. We cover the warning signs economists watch, the yield curve and the Sahm rule, including their 2022-2024 false alarms, then show what a recession does to jobs, interest rates, stocks and savings, with worked examples labeled as our own math. No predictions about the next recession.

0:00 Intro
0:42 What a recession is
1:57 The recession scoreboard
4:05 What causes a recession
6:12 The warning signs
7:46 What it does to your money
9:42 The recap

Sources: NBER, US Business Cycle Expansions and Contractions and Business Cycle Dating FAQ; NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee announcements (Dec 1, 2008; June 8, 2020); BEA, GDP Q2 2022 third estimate (Sept 2022); BLS unemployment rate data (annual averages 1990-2025; monthly peaks), BLS Employment Situation, September 2026 (Oct 2026); BLS, payroll employment April 2020; Federal Reserve History, Recession of 1981-82; CNBC (2023) and New York Fed yield curve model; Claudia Sahm on the Sahm rule; NBC News and Confluence Investment Management on 1970s oil prices; S&P 500 and Nasdaq drawdown data. Worked examples are our own math with stated assumptions.

News and education, not financial advice.

#recession #economy #personalfinance
